lesson.title: Two Traits at Once: Cracking the 9:3:3:1 Code
lesson.summary: A dihybrid cross tracks two genes at the same time, and Mendel's law of independent assortment predicts a signature 9:3:3:1 ratio of phenotypes among the offspring.
lesson.body:
A monohybrid cross follows one gene and one trait, but most organisms are being shaped by many genes simultaneously. A dihybrid cross follows two genes at once, and it works because of Mendel's law of independent assortment: as long as the two genes sit on different chromosomes, the allele a gamete receives for one gene has no effect on which allele it receives for the other gene. Each gene still segregates on its own, exactly as in a monohybrid cross. The two events just happen to occur together in the same organism.

Consider Mendel's own pea plants, tracking seed shape and seed color together. Round seed shape (R) is dominant over wrinkled (r), and yellow seed color (Y) is dominant over green (y). Cross two F1 plants that are heterozygous for both genes, RrYy by RrYy. Because the two genes assort independently, each parent produces four types of gametes in equal proportion: RY, Ry, rY, and ry, each at one quarter. That is simply the two monohybrid gamete pools, R or r and Y or y, combined in every possible pairing.

Laying those four gamete types across the top and down the side of a grid produces sixteen boxes. Sorting the resulting genotypes by phenotype gives nine boxes that are round and yellow, three that are round and green, three that are wrinkled and yellow, and one that is wrinkled and green. That 9:3:3:1 ratio out of sixteen is the signature of a dihybrid cross between two double heterozygotes, and it is close to what Mendel actually counted in his garden.

The ratio is not just a number to memorize. It is a direct consequence of two independent 3:1 ratios multiplying together, three quarters round times three quarters yellow gives nine sixteenths round and yellow, three quarters round times one quarter green gives three sixteenths round and green, and so on. Seeing the 9:3:3:1 pattern in real data is strong evidence that two genes are involved, that each shows simple dominance, and that the two genes assort independently of each other.
